title: Planning taxi shifts with trip data
introduction: The first proposed test is evening shift coverage. Compare airport and city pickup areas before moving vehicles.

context.audience: A historical case study for a taxi fleet manager.
context.decision: The decision: when and where should we test different shift coverage?
context.coverage: NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission yellow-taxi records, Jan–Mar 2025: 10.46 million trips after payment, fare and duration checks. This is citywide activity, not one company's fleet.
context.limitation: Recorded trips do not reveal unmet demand, idle vehicles or operating costs. These records cannot establish profit.

sections.title: 1. The starting point
sections.takeaway: Daily trips increased across the quarter. Daily averages make months of different lengths comparable.

charts.title: Average recorded trips per day
charts.reading_guide: One column per month; height shows its trip count divided by calendar days.
charts.caption: About 105,600 trips per day in January versus 124,100 in March. This establishes a busier historical baseline; it does not explain the increase or forecast the next quarter. Next, look at when those trips occurred.

sections.title: 2. When trips happen
sections.takeaway: Evenings are the first timing pattern to investigate. A small shift overlap is a more testable proposal than adding vehicles based on trip counts alone.

charts.title: Which hours were busiest?
charts.reading_guide: Read down for the hour and across for the weekday. Darker cells mean more recorded pickups in an average occurrence of that hour. Times are New York local time.
charts.caption: Thursday 6–7 pm averaged 10,289 pickups across the city; Friday 6–7 pm averaged 9,761. These are averages across the quarter, not counts for one date. A suggested test is a limited evening overlap, measuring pickup waits and net receipts per available vehicle-hour against unchanged shifts.

sections.title: 3. Where to compare
sections.takeaway: Airports generate large fares, but a long airport queue could offset that advantage. Compare an airport waiting location with a city pickup area before moving vehicles.

charts.title: Ten pickup areas with the most metered fares
charts.reading_guide: Longer bars mean a larger sum of meter fares from trips starting in that area. This measures fare volume, not the number of passengers or driver profit.
charts.caption: JFK contributed $24.33m and LaGuardia $11.49m. Yet Midtown Center had 485,609 trip records versus JFK's 383,928. An airport-versus-city test must include waiting, driving and repositioning time. The chart shows only the ten leading areas.

sections.title: 4. The everyday trips
sections.takeaway: Do not focus only on high fares. Trips with meter fares below $20 make up most recorded trips, so a city route remains a useful comparison for any airport test.

charts.title: How much did a typical trip cost on the meter?
charts.reading_guide: Each bar is the percentage of all eligible trip records in a meter-fare band. $10–<20 means at least $10 and less than $20. A fare band is not a distance band.
charts.caption: 44.71% of trips had meter fares from $10 to under $20; another 28.45% were below $10. High ticket size alone does not establish productivity. Meter fares exclude separate taxes, tolls, tips and surcharges.

sections.title: 5. Check the monthly mix
sections.takeaway: Airport contribution changes by month. Recheck the mix when evaluating a trial instead of assuming the same airport share all year.

charts.title: Where each month's meter fares came from
charts.reading_guide: Each cell is a percentage of that month's total meter fares. Read across a row to compare months. Use the printed percentages for the two airport rows; other pickup areas account for most fares.
charts.caption: JFK's share was 13.93% in January, 11.59% in February and 12.28% in March. These are shares of fares, not trips or profit. The next operational step is a small timing or location test with fresh data and measured costs—not a fleet-wide rollout from this historical quarter.
